mcqs.prompt: Which activity best prepares the platform for the peak?
mcqs.context: A retailer's e-commerce site faces a predictable seasonal surge in traffic and orders. The operations team must confirm the web tier can handle the projected peak requests per second, storage can absorb the added transaction volume, and enough support staff are scheduled to respond to incidents, all while continuing to meet the stated availability and recovery targets.

options.text: Capacity planning that models compute, storage, and staffing against the forecasted demand
options.rationale: Capacity planning sizes compute, storage, and people to the expected peak so the service meets its availability and recovery targets without over- or under-provisioning.

options.text: Purchasing the maximum server configuration available for every tier regardless of demand
options.rationale: Oversizing without analysis wastes budget and ignores staffing and storage sizing; capacity planning matches resources to measured demand instead.

options.text: Removing the load balancer so requests reach servers directly
options.rationale: Removing the load balancer eliminates distribution and failover, reducing availability exactly when peak demand arrives.

options.text: Extending the backup retention policy to cover the full peak period
options.rationale: Longer retention increases storage cost but does not size the platform for peak load or schedule staff; it addresses a different recovery requirement.

mcqs.hint: Forecast the expected workload, then size the infrastructure and the people needed to support it before the load arrives. The practice is about matching resources to measured demand rather than adding capacity after the fact.
mcqs.explanation: Capacity planning forecasts expected demand and sizes compute, storage, and staffing so the platform can meet its availability and recovery targets during peaks. Arbitrary oversizing wastes budget, removing load-balancing capacity reduces availability, and longer backup retention is a data-retention decision rather than load sizing.

mcqs.prompt: What should the network team do before mounting any access points?
mcqs.context: A hospital is adding Wi-Fi coverage for nursing tablets and VoIP handsets in a new wing. The team must guarantee continuous coverage while avoiding interference between access points and with nearby medical telemetry. The wing includes thick-walled rooms and a central elevator shaft that can shadow wireless signals.

options.text: Install access points at maximum transmit power to push coverage through walls
options.rationale: Running every AP at maximum power creates overlapping cells and co-channel interference, degrading throughput for all clients.

options.text: Perform a wireless site survey and analyze heat maps before placing access points
options.rationale: A site survey measures signal strength and coverage across the floor, and heat maps reveal weak and overlapping areas so APs can be positioned deliberately.

options.text: Place access points only where network cable is easiest to run
options.rationale: Cabling convenience does not account for radio coverage, so easy placement can leave dead zones in critical areas.

options.text: Mount the access points and rely on default channel assignments
options.rationale: Default channels cause adjacent APs to overlap on the same channel, increasing interference in a dense deployment.

mcqs.hint: Think about the planning step that produces a visual coverage analysis before any access point is permanently mounted.
mcqs.explanation: A wireless site survey collects signal measurements around the facility, and heat maps visualize coverage, interference, and dead zones, letting the team position access points and choose channels before mounting hardware. Maximum power and default channels worsen interference, while cabling convenience ignores radio physics.

sourceRefs.section: Objective 4.1 — Wireless security settings: Site surveys, Heat maps
NIST SP 800-153 — Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (site survey)

mcqs.prompt: Which TWO cookie attributes should the team set to address these findings? (Select TWO.)
mcqs.context: A financial services web application stores the session identifier in a cookie. A penetration test found two issues: a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw that lets an attacker read document.cookie, and a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) flaw that lets an attacker trigger state-changing requests while the victim's session is active. The application is already served exclusively over HTTPS.

options.rationale: HttpOnly prevents client-side scripts from reading the cookie, blocking the XSS-based session theft.
SameSite restricts the browser from attaching the cookie to cross-site requests, mitigating the CSRF flaw.
The Secure attribute only forces HTTPS delivery, which the site already guarantees, so it adds no protection here.

options.text: Domain set to the parent domain
options.rationale: Broadening the Domain scope sends the cookie to more hosts, enlarging the attack surface rather than hardening it.

options.text: A long Max-Age for persistent sessions
options.rationale: Lengthening the cookie's life increases the window in which a stolen or leaked session can be replayed.
SameSite=None explicitly permits cross-site sending of the cookie, directly worsening the CSRF exposure.

mcqs.hint: Separate the two attack types: one attribute keeps the cookie out of client-side script, the other limits when the browser attaches the cookie to requests from other sites.
mcqs.explanation: HttpOnly denies JavaScript access to the cookie, defeating the XSS exfiltration, while SameSite stops the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests, defeating CSRF. Secure is redundant on an HTTPS-only site, and expanding domain scope, extending lifetime, or allowing cross-site sending increases exposure rather than reducing it. Why the other options fail: A long Max-Age for persistent sessions: Lengthening the cookie's life increases the window in which a stolen or leaked session can be replayed.

sourceRefs.section: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite attributes

mcqs.prompt: Which technique would the team add to the pipeline to inspect the source code itself before the application is built or executed?
mcqs.context: A development team wants to catch injection, cross-site scripting, and buffer-overflow flaws before code is deployed. They plan to add a scanning step to their CI pipeline that runs automatically on every commit. The team's budget covers one new tool, and the tool must not require a running, instrumented application.

options.rationale: SAST examines source code without executing it, catching flaws early in CI before deployment.
DAST probes a running application over HTTP, so it requires a deployed or staged instance rather than analyzing source.
Fuzzing executes the program with malformed inputs to trigger crashes, which needs a runnable build, not static inspection.
Penetration testing is a manual or semi-automated exercise against live systems, not a per-commit source inspection.

mcqs.hint: Contrast reading the code itself with techniques that require a running application and live input.
mcqs.explanation: Static code analysis parses the source and models data flow to find vulnerabilities such as injection, XSS, and buffer overflows before anything runs, which fits a per-commit CI gate. DAST, fuzzing, and penetration testing all act against an executed application and would come later in the lifecycle.

sourceRefs.section: Objective 4.1 — Application security: Static code analysis

mcqs.prompt: Which TWO approaches should the team use together to enumerate the organization's assets? (Select TWO.)
mcqs.context: An organization is building a complete hardware and software asset inventory to identify unmanaged and rogue devices before an upcoming security audit. Endpoint agents are installed on most laptops, but the team cannot assume coverage is complete because servers, network gear, and IoT devices were never enrolled. The inventory must reflect what is actually connected today.

options.text: Active network scanning across all subnets to discover hosts, ports, and services
options.rationale: Network scanning directly discovers connected devices, including ones with no agent, providing a live view of the environment.

options.text: Correlating the CMDB, DHCP leases, and directory service records
options.rationale: Authoritative records of known systems and address assignments reveal managed assets and help reconcile the scan results.

options.text: Using only the agent data already collected from managed laptops
options.rationale: Agent-only data misses servers, network gear, IoT, and rogue devices, so the inventory stays incomplete.

options.text: Purging inventory records older than 90 days to reduce noise
options.rationale: Deleting historical records removes visibility into assets that may still be active and connected.

options.text: Restricting discovery to the finance department's subnet
options.rationale: Scoping to one subnet leaves every other segment unexplored, defeating the purpose of a full inventory.

options.text: Waiting for the next annual audit to compile the list
options.rationale: A once-a-year snapshot cannot support ongoing asset tracking or reveal what is connected today.

mcqs.hint: Combine a technique that sees devices directly on the network with the organization's existing authoritative records of systems and addresses.
mcqs.explanation: Active scanning discovers what is actually on the wire, while CMDB, DHCP, and directory records provide context on known assets; together they reconcile managed, unmanaged, and rogue devices. Agent-only, subnet-limited, record-purging, or annual approaches each leave material gaps in the inventory. Why the other options fail: Restricting discovery to the finance department's subnet: Scoping to one subnet leaves every other segment unexplored, defeating the purpose of a full inventory.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-115 — Technical Guide to Information Security Testing (network discovery and enumeration)

mcqs.prompt: Which term best describes the researcher's action?
mcqs.context: A security researcher discovers a critical remote code execution flaw in a company's web portal. The company operates a public bug bounty program with a defined scope and rules of engagement. The researcher reports the flaw privately through the program, the vendor confirms it and schedules a patch, and the researcher agrees to keep the details confidential until the fix is released, when a public advisory will be published.

options.rationale: The researcher privately reports, the vendor fixes within a negotiated window, and details are published only after remediation — the defining pattern of coordinated disclosure.
Full disclosure publishes vulnerability details and proof of concept immediately to force a response, the opposite of this embargoed process.
Selling the flaw to a third party without notifying the vendor does not match a private report through the vendor's own program.
Demanding payment to keep the vulnerability secret differs from reporting through a program that the company itself operates.

mcqs.hint: Compare what the researcher did — private report, vendor fix window, then public advisory — with models that publish immediately or withhold details for gain.
mcqs.explanation: Coordinated (responsible) disclosure gives the vendor a chance to remediate before the public learns of the flaw, and the bug bounty program is the channel through which the report flowed. Full disclosure, exploit brokering, and extortion all lack the vendor-remediation-first sequence.

sourceRefs.section: Objective 4.3 — Identification methods: Responsible disclosure program, Bug bounty program
Responsible Disclosure and Bug Bounty Programs

mcqs.prompt: What is the primary security value of this dark-web intelligence?
mcqs.context: The security team subscribes to a dark-web monitoring service. An analyst finds the CTO's corporate email address and a password hash posted on a criminal forum, along with chatter advertising access to the company's VPN. The team has no current evidence of intrusion, but the data appears to match credentials exposed in a recent phishing campaign.

options.text: It gives early warning to reset exposed credentials and hunt for unauthorized access
options.rationale: Leaked credentials and access chatter let the team rotate passwords, block compromised accounts, and search logs for signs the access was used.

options.text: It confirms the CTO's account is actively compromised
options.rationale: A posted hash indicates exposure, not that the account has already been used; the team must still investigate.
Dark-web monitoring addresses credential exposure and threat chatter, not software vulnerabilities, so scanning remains necessary.

options.text: It provides court-admissible evidence of the attacker's identity
options.rationale: Monitoring feeds are intelligence leads, not forensic evidence; attribution requires a proper investigation.

mcqs.hint: Focus on what the intelligence lets the team do before an incident occurs — invalidate exposed credentials and check whether leaked access was already used.
mcqs.explanation: Dark-web monitoring is a threat-intelligence source: finding posted credentials and access chatter enables proactive resets and threat hunting. It does not by itself prove compromise, and it complements rather than replaces vulnerability scanning or forensic investigation. Why the other options fail: It confirms the CTO's account is actively compromised: A posted hash indicates exposure, not that the account has already been used; the team must still investigate; It provides court-admissible evidence of the attacker's identity: Monitoring feeds are intelligence leads, not forensic evidence; attribution requires a proper investigation.

sourceRefs.section: Objective 4.3 — Identification methods: Dark web, Threat feed
NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

mcqs.prompt: Which set of standards would the team rely on to automate these checks under SCAP?
mcqs.context: A compliance team must assess thousands of servers against a published hardening benchmark, remediate failures, and produce auditable evidence. To do this at scale, they adopt the Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) so the checks are machine-readable and repeatable rather than manual.

options.text: XCCDF for the benchmark/policy, OVAL for the technical checks, and CVE for vulnerability identifiers
options.rationale: XCCDF expresses the checklist and results, OVAL defines machine-readable tests of system state, and CVE names vulnerabilities — the core SCAP components.

options.text: STIX, TAXII, and OpenIOC for threat-intelligence sharing
options.rationale: These are threat-intelligence exchange formats, not configuration-assessment standards, so they do not automate benchmark checks.

options.text: NetFlow, SNMP traps, and syslog for network monitoring
options.rationale: These collect traffic and device events; they report activity but do not assess configuration against a benchmark.

options.text: DMARC, DKIM, and SPF for email authentication
options.rationale: Email authentication protocols protect mail delivery, unrelated to server configuration assessment.

mcqs.hint: Recall that SCAP pairs a policy/benchmark language with a machine-readable check language and a shared vulnerability naming standard.
mcqs.explanation: SCAP bundles XCCDF (checklists and results), OVAL (system-state checks), and CVE (vulnerability identifiers), along with CPE and CVSS, to automate and standardize configuration assessment. The other options are threat-intelligence, monitoring, or email protocols outside SCAP's scope.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-126 — The Technical Specification for the Security Content Automation Protocol

mcqs.prompt: Which configuration would give the team immediate, event-driven alerts without polling?
mcqs.context: The network operations team needs to know the moment a core switch fails, an interface goes down, or a router restarts so they can respond before users notice. Their monitoring server currently polls devices on a five-minute cycle, which is too slow for critical infrastructure.

options.text: Configure SNMP traps so managed devices send unsolicited notifications to the monitoring server
options.rationale: SNMP traps push event notifications the instant a device detects a condition, enabling immediate alerting without polling.

options.text: Shorten the SNMP polling interval to every few seconds
options.rationale: More frequent polling still relies on the server requesting state, adds load to devices and the network, and can miss short-lived events.

options.text: Enable NetFlow export on the switches
options.rationale: NetFlow records traffic flows for analysis; it does not report device faults such as a switch rebooting.

options.text: Disable SNMP and rely on manual checks
options.rationale: Removing SNMP eliminates automated visibility entirely and delays detection of failures.

mcqs.hint: Distinguish messages a device pushes the moment an event occurs from state collected through repeated requests or flow sampling.
mcqs.explanation: SNMP traps are unsolicited notifications sent by managed devices when an event such as a link failure or restart occurs, giving near-real-time alerting. Polling, NetFlow, or disabling SNMP each fail to deliver event-driven fault alerts.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-123 — Guide to General Server Security (network monitoring and SNMP)

mcqs.prompt: Which statement best describes SELinux and how the team should use it?
mcqs.context: A Linux web server hosts an application that was breached last year after the web daemon's process was used to read sensitive files. The security team enables SELinux so that even if the application is compromised, it is confined. During rollout, the application fails to start because SELinux denies one of its legitimate operations, and an administrator proposes switching the server to permissive mode.

options.text: Keep enforcing mode and use permissive mode only temporarily to identify denials from the audit log
options.rationale: Enforcing mode blocks policy violations; permissive mode logs without blocking, so it is useful only for troubleshooting before returning to enforcing.

options.text: Switch to permissive mode permanently because it blocks violations while allowing the app to run
options.rationale: Permissive mode does not block anything — it only logs denials, so it provides no real confinement.

options.text: Disable SELinux because the firewall already protects the server
options.rationale: A firewall filters network traffic; SELinux confines local processes, so disabling it removes the protection that would limit a compromised daemon.

options.text: Replace standard file permissions with SELinux labels
options.rationale: SELinux adds mandatory access control on top of DAC; it does not replace ownership and permission bits.

mcqs.hint: Think about what mandatory access control adds beyond the firewall and file permissions, and what each SELinux mode actually does with a violation.
mcqs.explanation: SELinux applies mandatory access control so a process is confined by policy even when it runs with elevated privileges; enforcing mode blocks violations while permissive mode only logs them. The administrator should allow the legitimate operation in policy and remain in enforcing mode, rather than disable the control.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-123 — Guide to General Server Security (mandatory access control)

mcqs.prompt: Which IAM process is the team performing?
mcqs.context: Before issuing credentials to a newly hired remote contractor, the IAM team must confirm the contractor is genuinely who they claim to be. The contractor uploads a government-issued ID, the system compares it with a live selfie, and the contractor answers knowledge-based questions from public records. Only after this passes does the system issue the account.

options.rationale: Identity proofing verifies a person's claimed identity at enrollment using documents and other evidence before credentials are issued.
Authorization assigns what an identified user may access; it assumes identity has already been established.
Federation establishes trust between identity providers so one organization accepts another's assertions, not the initial identity check.
Accounting records and audits user activity after access exists; it does not verify who the user is at enrollment.

mcqs.hint: Consider which step establishes that a person is who they claim to be before any credentials or permissions are issued.
mcqs.explanation: Identity proofing validates the applicant's identity through identity documents, biometric comparison, and knowledge-based verification before account issuance. Authorization, federation, and accounting all operate after or alongside an established identity.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-63A — Digital Identity Guidelines: Enrollment and Identity Proofing

mcqs.prompt: What is this mechanism called?
mcqs.context: An organization allows only company-issued laptops onto the VPN. Each laptop's Trusted Platform Module (TPM) records measurements of the firmware and boot process, signs a statement about those measurements, and presents it to the VPN gateway. The gateway verifies the signature and the measurements before permitting the connection, rejecting devices whose boot state has been altered.

options.rationale: Attestation is a party proving to a verifier that its hardware and software are in a trusted, expected state, here via TPM-signed boot measurements.
Federation links identity providers for single sign-on; it does not prove a device's boot state.
Non-repudiation prevents denying that an action took place; it does not validate the integrity of a device's boot state.
Port-based (802.1X) authentication controls network access by credentials but does not verify measured boot state.

mcqs.hint: Focus on the term for a device proving to a verifier that its hardware and software are in a trusted, expected state.
mcqs.explanation: Attestation lets a device demonstrate its state to a verifier: the TPM signs the measured boot values and the VPN gateway checks them, blocking tampered devices. Federation, non-repudiation, and port-based authentication address different problems.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-63B — Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management (attestation)

mcqs.prompt: What is the primary security advantage of this passwordless approach?
mcqs.context: An organization replaces passwords with FIDO2 passkeys for all employees. Users unlock sign-in on their device with a biometric or PIN, and the private key is generated and stored in the device's secure element. When a user signs in to a site, the site's challenge is answered with the device-bound key rather than a shared secret typed by the user.

options.text: There is no reusable shared secret to phish or steal, because the private key never leaves the user's device
options.rationale: Passkeys eliminate the shared-secret model: the private key stays in the device, and a phished site cannot replay it.

options.text: Users can now use one master password for every site
options.rationale: Passkeys remove the password entirely; a shared master password would recreate the same credential-theft risk.

options.text: The private key is backed up on the server so users can recover it
options.rationale: Exporting the private key to servers recreates a shared secret and defeats the device-bound security model.

options.text: One-time codes delivered by SMS are more resistant to phishing
options.rationale: SMS one-time codes remain phishable and are subject to SIM-swap attacks, unlike device-bound passkeys.

mcqs.hint: Consider what an attacker would need to phish or steal when authentication uses a private key that never leaves the user's device.
mcqs.explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys bind the private key to the device and use origin-bound challenges, so there is no password or reusable code for attackers to phish. Server-side key storage or SMS codes each reintroduce the shared-secret weaknesses passkeys remove.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-63B — Digital Identity Guidelines (phishing-resistant authenticators)

mcqs.prompt: Which access control is the company implementing?
mcqs.context: A retailer's back-office systems process payroll and inventory only during store hours. The IAM policy prevents administrative accounts from authenticating between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. local time, when no store employees are scheduled. A night-shift cleaner's badge is also blocked from entering the office floor outside those same hours.

options.rationale: Time-of-day restrictions limit when authentication or physical access is permitted based on the clock, matching the company's operating schedule.
Account lockout disables accounts after failed attempts; it does not restrict access by the time of day.
A session timeout ends an idle session after a period of inactivity; it does not prevent access during certain hours.
Geolocation restricts access by physical location, not by time.

mcqs.hint: Identify the access rule that constrains when authentication or access is permitted according to the clock.
mcqs.explanation: Time-of-day restrictions encode business-hours access in the IAM policy, so accounts cannot authenticate outside the permitted window — applied here to both logical and physical access. Lockout, timeout, and geolocation address different access dimensions.

mcqs.prompt: Which TWO statements best describe this ephemeral credential approach? (Select TWO.)
mcqs.context: A security team removes standing administrative rights from all IT staff and deploys a privileged access management tool. When an administrator needs elevated rights, they submit a request with a justification, the tool grants temporary credentials that expire after 15 minutes, and the rights are automatically removed. Every grant and use is recorded.

options.text: Credentials are short-lived and expire automatically, eliminating the need for manual revocation
options.rationale: Ephemeral credentials self-expire in minutes, so the standing-privilege window and manual revocation burden disappear.

options.text: Privilege is granted per request, shrinking the attack surface available at any moment
options.rationale: Just-in-time grants mean elevated rights exist only while a task requires them, reducing exposure.

options.text: Credentials remain valid indefinitely to avoid re-enrollment overhead
options.rationale: Long-lived credentials recreate the standing-privilege risk the team is removing.

options.text: The same standing rights remain available 24/7 through the tool
options.rationale: Always-on elevated rights defeat the purpose of just-in-time access.

options.text: Audit logging is disabled to reduce storage costs
options.rationale: Removing the audit trail destroys the accountability that makes ephemeral access safe to grant.

options.text: Credentials are embedded in shared scripts for convenience
options.rationale: Storing credentials in scripts exposes secrets to anyone who reads the script.

mcqs.hint: Think about the two properties that remove standing privilege: the credential window is very short, and elevated access appears only when a task actually needs it.
mcqs.explanation: Ephemeral credentials expire automatically, and just-in-time provisioning grants privilege only for the active task, so attackers cannot harvest always-on admin rights. Indefinite validity, standing rights, embedded secrets, and disabled logging all undermine the model.

sourceRefs.section: Objective 4.6 — Privileged access management tools: Just-in-time permissions, Ephemeral credentials
NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture (short-lived credentials)

mcqs.prompt: What must the organization do to satisfy this legal hold?
mcqs.context: A company receives a litigation hold notice after a former employee sues the firm over a disputed contract. The notice covers email, chat, and file-share content related to the contract. The company's data-retention policy normally deletes email after 90 days, and backups are recycled every four weeks.

options.text: Preserve all potentially relevant data, suspend routine deletion, and protect backups until the hold is lifted
options.rationale: A legal hold freezes normal retention: relevant data, including backups and archives, must be preserved to avoid spoliation.

options.text: Continue the 90-day retention schedule to reduce storage costs
options.rationale: Deleting on schedule while a hold is active destroys evidence and can expose the company to sanctions for spoliation.

options.text: Encrypt and then permanently delete the contract-related data
options.rationale: Destroying the very data in dispute guarantees loss of evidence and violates the hold.

options.text: Take no action until a court orders specific documents
options.rationale: The hold notice itself already triggers the preservation obligation; waiting risks automatic deletion before any order arrives.

mcqs.hint: The hold flips the normal lifecycle rule: instead of deleting on schedule, the organization must freeze and protect the relevant records, including backups.
mcqs.explanation: E-discovery and legal hold require preserving potentially relevant data — email, chat, file shares, and backups — and suspending routine destruction until the hold is lifted. Continuing deletions or destroying the data constitutes spoliation and undermines any investigation. Why the other options fail: Continue the 90-day retention schedule to reduce storage costs: Deleting on schedule while a hold is active destroys evidence and can expose the company to sanctions for spoliation.

sourceRefs.section: NIST SP 800-86 — Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response (legal hold and preservation)

mcqs.prompt: Which metric is the best leading key risk indicator (KRI) for this board-level reporting?
mcqs.context: A regional credit union's CISO prepares a quarterly risk dashboard for the board of directors. The board wants early-warning signals that security risk is increasing before incidents occur, so leadership can intervene while conditions can still be changed. The CISO is selecting metrics from the current vulnerability, access, and incident data.

options.text: Percentage of internet-facing systems with known critical CVEs that remain unpatched beyond the remediation SLA
options.rationale: A high or rising percentage signals growing exposure to exploitation before an incident occurs, making it a leading indicator that management can still act on.

options.text: Number of confirmed security incidents reported in the previous quarter
options.rationale: Incident counts describe what already happened, so they are lagging indicators rather than forward-looking KRIs.

options.text: Total security budget expended during the current fiscal year
options.rationale: Spending levels track finance, not the level of exposure or the likelihood of future harm.

options.text: Number of employees who completed the annual security awareness course
options.rationale: Training completion is an activity measure and does not directly signal rising exposure to a specific risk.

mcqs.hint: A leading KRI rises or falls with exposure before damage occurs. Ask whether each metric predicts future risk that leadership can still influence, rather than merely recording past events.
mcqs.explanation: The percentage of internet-facing systems with unpatched critical CVEs is a leading KRI: it rises as remediation falls behind, signaling greater likelihood of exploitation while corrective action is still possible. Confirmed incidents are lagging indicators that report past outcomes. Budget figures measure spending rather than exposure, and training completion tracks activity instead of current risk level. Effective KRIs are measurable, tied to a specific risk, and give the board time to respond. Why the other options fail: Number of employees who completed the annual security awareness course: Training completion is an activity measure and does not directly signal rising exposure to a specific risk.

sourceRefs.section: Risk Register and Key Risk Indicators

mcqs.prompt: Which TWO actions correctly handle this conflict of interest? (Select TWO.)
mcqs.context: A mid-sized insurer hires an independent security firm to assess a prospective cloud vendor's controls before signing a contract. During kickoff, the assessment lead reveals that she owns shares in the vendor and previously consulted for them. The insurer's third-party risk policy requires unbiased vendor evaluations, and the vendor agreement includes a right-to-audit clause.

options.text: Disclose the relationship to the insurer and recuse the assessor from the engagement
options.rationale: Disclosing the interest and removing the assessor from the evaluation preserves the independence the assessment requires.

options.text: Replace the assessment team with personnel who have no personal or financial ties to the vendor
options.rationale: Assigning unconflicted assessors eliminates the conflict at the source and keeps the evaluation objective.

options.text: Let the assessor proceed because personal holdings do not affect technical findings
options.rationale: An undisclosed financial interest can bias conclusions, so allowing participation without disclosure violates due diligence.

options.text: Document the conflict in the final report after the evaluation is complete
options.rationale: Disclosure after the fact does not remove the conflicted assessor's influence over the findings, so it fails to restore independence.

options.text: Waive the conflict because the vendor has a strong compliance record
options.rationale: A vendor's reputation does not neutralize an assessor's personal interest; an independent evaluation is still required.

options.text: Allow participation but instruct the assessor to remain objective
options.rationale: An instruction cannot offset a financial interest; the standard practice is recusal or replacement.

mcqs.hint: Independence is the point of third-party assessment. Think about actions that remove the conflicted person's influence before the work begins, rather than attempts to manage or explain the interest afterward.
mcqs.explanation: Conflict-of-interest handling in vendor assessment comes down to preserving independence: the interested assessor should be recused (a), and ideally the team replaced with people who have no ties to the vendor (b). Proceeding without disclosure (c), documenting the conflict only after the report is written (d), waiving it because of the vendor's record (e), or promising objectivity (f) all leave the conflicted party's influence in place and undermine the due-diligence value of the assessment.

mcqs.prompt: Which security objective is the hospital enforcing?

options.rationale: Non-repudiation: Prevents a party from denying that they performed an action, typically enforced with digital signatures. Confidentiality is the concept the scenario tests, not Non-repudiation.
Confidentiality: Ensures data is accessible only to authorized parties and is protected from unauthorized disclosure or exposure.
Availability: Ensures that authorized users can access systems and data when needed. It does not provide Confidentiality, which is what the scenario asks for.
Integrity: Guarantees that data has not been altered or tampered with and remains accurate and complete. The requirement is Confidentiality; this option supplies Integrity instead.

mcqs.explanation: Confidentiality: Ensures data is accessible only to authorized parties and is protected from unauthorized disclosure or exposure. The requirement is about who may view the data. It says nothing about whether the record was altered or whether the service stayed online. The remaining choices describe different concepts: Availability — Ensures that authorized users can access systems and data when needed; Integrity — Guarantees that data has not been altered or tampered with and remains accurate and complete; Non-repudiation — Prevents a party from denying that they performed an action, typically enforced with digital signatures.

mcqs.prompt: Which property does the digital signature provide in this dispute?

options.rationale: Confidentiality: Ensures data is accessible only to authorized parties and is protected from unauthorized disclosure or exposure. This option is Confidentiality, which is not the property or control the scenario asks for.

The distractors describe different concepts: Confidentiality — Ensures data is accessible only to authorized parties and is protected from unauthorized disclosure or exposure; Authentication — The process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or system; Integrity — Guarantees that data has not been altered or tampered with and remains accurate and complete.

mcqs.prompt: Which framework is the gateway implementing?

options.rationale: AAA: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting: the framework for controlling and tracking access to resources.

mcqs.explanation: AAA: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting: the framework for controlling and tracking access to resources. Three distinct jobs are in play: proving who the user is, deciding what the user may reach, and recording what happened. Each distractor belongs to another concept family: Authorization — The process of granting or denying access to a resource based on the authenticated identity; Accounting — The process of logging and tracking user actions and resource usage for auditing and billing; Authentication — The process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or system.

mcqs.prompt: A ____ function such as SHA-256 produces a fixed-length digest used to verify ____, while a ____ uses a private key to prove non-repudiation.
mcqs.explanation: The correct chips are hashing (Function), integrity (Property), digital signature (Mechanism). Hashing matches the 'Function' blank; integrity matches the 'Property' blank; and digital signature matches the 'Mechanism' blank. Hashing is a one-way function that produces a fixed-length digest. Integrity is the property that data has not been altered. Digital signature is a value created with a private key that proves origin and integrity. SaaS is a cloud service model, not a cryptographic primitive. Tokenization is replacing sensitive data with an unrelated surrogate, so it does not complete any blank.
mcqs.hint: Name the job each blank performs before looking at the chips: a one-way function, the property it protects, and a private-key mechanism that proves origin.

mcqs.prompt: The CIA triad is made up of ____, ____, and ____.
mcqs.explanation: The correct chips are confidentiality (C), integrity (I), availability (A). Confidentiality matches the 'C' blank; integrity matches the 'I' blank; and availability matches the 'A' blank. Confidentiality is the property that only authorized parties can view data. Integrity is the property that data has not been altered. Availability is the property that authorized users can reach systems and data. MAC is an access model, not one of the three core properties. Risk acceptance is a risk treatment, not a risk metric or a security property.

Input validation: Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws. It does not provide Stack canary, which is what the scenario asks for.
Secure boot: Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next. It does not provide Stack canary, which is what the scenario asks for.
ASLR: Address Space Layout Randomization: randomizes memory addresses to hinder exploitation. ASLR would fit a different scenario than the Stack canary requirement here.

mcqs.explanation: Stack canary: A sentinel value that detects buffer overflows before they overwrite the return address. A sentinel value reveals that the saved return address is about to be overwritten. The defense is not address randomization or non-executable memory. The remaining choices describe different concepts: Secure boot — Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next; ASLR — Address Space Layout Randomization: randomizes memory addresses to hinder exploitation; Input validation — Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws.
mcqs.hint: A sentinel value reveals that the saved return address is about to be overwritten. The defense is not address randomization or non-executable memory.
mcqs.context: A compiler option inserts a known value between a local buffer and the saved return address. Before a function returns, the generated code compares the value and aborts if it changed. A developer is naming the overflow defense that just triggered.

mcqs.prompt: Which boot-integrity feature is the server using?

options.rationale: Stack canary: A sentinel value that detects buffer overflows before they overwrite the return address. The keyed requirement is Secure boot; Stack canary does not satisfy it.
Measured boot: Recording hashes of each boot stage to a TPM for later attestation of integrity. It does not provide Secure boot, which is what the scenario asks for.
Input validation: Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws. Secure boot is the concept the scenario tests, not Input validation.
Secure boot: Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next.

mcqs.explanation: Secure boot: Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next. Each stage verifies the signature of the next stage before handing over control. The feature blocks execution rather than only recording measurements. Each alternative belongs to a different concept family: Measured boot — Recording hashes of each boot stage to a TPM for later attestation of integrity; Stack canary — A sentinel value that detects buffer overflows before they overwrite the return address; Input validation — Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws.
mcqs.hint: Each stage verifies the signature of the next stage before handing over control. The feature blocks execution rather than only recording measurements.
mcqs.context: A server firmware checks the signature of the bootloader before running it, and the bootloader checks the signature of the kernel. If any signature is invalid, the chain stops and the machine refuses to boot. The platform engineer is naming the boot protection.

mcqs.prompt: Which boot-integrity feature is the laptop using?

options.rationale: Parameterized queries: Using bound parameters so user input is treated as data, not executable SQL. The scenario's requirement is Measured boot; this option is Parameterized queries.
Input validation: Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws. The scenario's requirement is Measured boot; this option is Input validation.
Secure boot: Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next. The scenario's requirement is Measured boot; this option is Secure boot.
Measured boot: Recording hashes of each boot stage to a TPM for later attestation of integrity.

mcqs.explanation: Measured boot: Recording hashes of each boot stage to a TPM for later attestation of integrity. The boot chain records values for later comparison. It does not stop the boot when a measurement differs. The distractors describe different concepts: Secure boot — Cryptographically verifying each boot component before executing the next; Input validation — Rejecting malformed input at the boundary to prevent injection and overflow flaws; Parameterized queries — Using bound parameters so user input is treated as data, not executable SQL.
mcqs.hint: The boot chain records values for later comparison. It does not stop the boot when a measurement differs.
mcqs.context: A laptop records a hash of each boot component into a hardware chip and later sends those measurements to a management server. The server compares the values with a known-good baseline but the laptop still boots when a value differs. The endpoint team is naming the feature.

mcqs.prompt: Which browser security header is the application using?

options.rationale: DLP: Data Loss Prevention: controls that detect and block exfiltration of sensitive data. This option is DLP, which is not the property or control the scenario asks for.
NAC: Network Access Control: enforces policy on devices before allowing them onto the network. NAC would fit a different scenario than the CSP requirement here.
Syslog: A standard protocol for sending and collecting system log messages, often to a central server. The scenario calls for CSP, so Syslog is the wrong concept.
CSP: Content Security Policy: an HTTP header that restricts which scripts and sources a page may load.

mcqs.explanation: CSP: Content Security Policy: an HTTP header that restricts which scripts and sources a page may load. The header restricts which sources a page may load. It is not a server-side query parameterization or a cookie flag. The remaining choices describe different concepts: NAC — Network Access Control: enforces policy on devices before allowing them onto the network; Syslog — A standard protocol for sending and collecting system log messages, often to a central server; DLP — Data Loss Prevention: controls that detect and block exfiltration of sensitive data.
mcqs.hint: The header restricts which sources a page may load. It is not a server-side query parameterization or a cookie flag.
mcqs.context: A web application returns a header that lists the only origins allowed to load scripts, styles, and frames. When an injected script tries to run from an unlisted source, the browser blocks it. The developer is naming the header.

mcqs.prompt: A company is moving from a perimeter-based model to zero trust. Which principle should guide the NEW architecture above all others?

options.text: Never trust, always verify every request
options.rationale: Correct choice — Never trust, always verify every request: Zero trust is defined by 'never trust, always verify' and assumes breach.

options.text: Place the firewall at the largest network boundary
options.rationale: A single perimeter firewall still trusts everything inside it and does not verify each request.

options.text: Trust all internal traffic by default
options.rationale: Trusting internal traffic is the perimeter assumption that zero trust replaces.
Removing a factor weakens authentication and does not verify every request.

mcqs.explanation: Zero trust is defined by 'never trust, always verify' and assumes breach; perimeter trust is the old model it replaces. Why the other options fail: Place the firewall at the largest network boundary — A single perimeter firewall still trusts everything inside it and does not verify each request.; Trust all internal traffic by default — Trusting internal traffic is the perimeter assumption that zero trust replaces.; Disable multi-factor authentication for speed — Removing a factor weakens authentication and does not verify every request.
mcqs.hint: The old model trusted anything inside the perimeter. The new rule must apply to every request, not just external ones.
mcqs.context: A company is retiring its assumption that traffic inside the office is trustworthy. The new architecture must authenticate and authorize every request, encrypt traffic between services, and limit each workload to the resources it actually needs. The architect is choosing the principle that should guide every design decision.

mcqs.prompt: A web application accepts user input and builds SQL from string concatenation. Which control would BEST prevent the resulting class of attack?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Parameterized queries: Parameterized queries treat input as data, defeating SQL injection.
Disk encryption protects data at rest; it does not stop SQL injection at the query layer.
Segmentation limits lateral movement; it does not keep user input from becoming SQL code.
Training changes user behavior over time; it does not keep user input from becoming SQL code.

mcqs.explanation: Parameterized queries treat input as data, defeating SQL injection. Why the other options fail: Disk encryption — Disk encryption protects data at rest; it does not stop SQL injection at the query layer.; Network segmentation — Segmentation limits lateral movement; it does not keep user input from becoming SQL code.; Security awareness training — Training changes user behavior over time; it does not keep user input from becoming SQL code.
mcqs.hint: The flaw is that user text becomes SQL code. The fix must keep code and values separate at the database boundary.
mcqs.context: A web application builds a database query by concatenating the submitted account number with SQL text. A tester enters a quote and a boolean expression and receives every customer row. The developer is choosing the control that removes the vulnerability at its source.

mcqs.prompt: Which control is MOST appropriate?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Dual control: Dual control requires two authorized people for a sensitive action.
Complexity rules make guessing harder but do not require a second person to approve a transfer.
Audit logging records actions after they occur; it does not require a second person to approve a transaction.
Antivirus matches known malicious files or behavior on an endpoint; it does not orchestrate multi-tool response.

mcqs.explanation: Dual control requires two authorized people for a sensitive action; the others do not enforce two-person integrity. Why the other options fail: Password complexity — Complexity rules make guessing harder but do not require a second person to approve a transfer.; Audit logging — Audit logging records actions after they occur; it does not require a second person to approve a transaction.; Antivirus — Antivirus matches known malicious files or behavior on an endpoint; it does not orchestrate multi-tool response.
mcqs.hint: One person can start the transfer and a different person must release it. Look for the control that requires both actions.
mcqs.context: A payment platform requires one administrator to initiate a wire transfer and a different administrator to approve it. Neither administrator can complete both steps, even if both know the procedure and hold valid credentials. The auditor is naming the control that enforces the split.

mcqs.prompt: Which attack is MOST likely?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Spear phishing: Personalized, context-aware email targeting a specific person is spear phishing.
Generic phishing is a broad campaign; the described message is personalized for one employee.
Vishing uses a voice call; the described lure arrives by email or text.
Smishing delivers a lure by text message; it does not describe a forged memory address.

mcqs.explanation: Personalized, context-aware email targeting a specific person is spear phishing; whaling targets executives specifically. Why the other options fail: Generic phishing — Generic phishing is a broad campaign; the described message is personalized for one employee.; Vishing — Vishing uses a voice call; the described lure arrives by email or text.; Smishing — Smishing delivers a lure by text message; it does not describe a forged memory address.
mcqs.hint: The message is personalized with a manager, a real invoice, and a single recipient. That narrow targeting is the clue.
mcqs.context: An accounts-payable employee receives an email that names her manager, cites a real invoice number, and asks her to change a vendor's bank details before the afternoon payment run. The message is addressed only to her and uses details from a recent project thread.

mcqs.prompt: What type of attack is MOST likely occurring?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Brute force: Rapid repeated failures then success indicates brute force.
A distributed denial-of-service flood exhausts availability; it does not test credentials or capture a session.
A relay attack requires an attacker between two parties; a noise flood denies service without relaying traffic.
SQL injection manipulates a database query; it does not forge a domain-wide authentication ticket.

mcqs.explanation: Rapid repeated failures then success indicates brute force; password spraying tries few passwords across many accounts. Why the other options fail: DDoS — A distributed denial-of-service flood exhausts availability; it does not test credentials or capture a session.; MITM — A relay attack requires an attacker between two parties; a noise flood denies service without relaying traffic.; SQL injection — SQL injection manipulates a database query; it does not forge a domain-wide authentication ticket.
mcqs.hint: Many failures against one account in a short window suggest exhaustive guessing rather than a list or a wide spray.
mcqs.context: A SOC sees hundreds of failed logins from one address in two minutes, followed by a success. The attempts cycle through a short list of common values against the same account. The analyst is classifying the attack.

mcqs.prompt: Which wireless attack uses noise to deny service across the band?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Jamming: Jamming is Layer 1 denial of service by noise.
An evil twin impersonates a legitimate access point; it does not flood the frequency with noise.
A rogue access point is unauthorized; a noise flood is not an access point at all.
A disassociation flood drops wireless associations; it does not broadcast a look-alike network name.

mcqs.explanation: Jamming is Layer 1 denial of service by noise; an evil twin/spoofs a fake AP rather than drowning the signal. Why the other options fail: Evil twin — An evil twin impersonates a legitimate access point; it does not flood the frequency with noise.; Rogue AP — A rogue access point is unauthorized; a noise flood is not an access point at all.; Disassociation — A disassociation flood drops wireless associations; it does not broadcast a look-alike network name.
mcqs.hint: The interference covers the whole band and affects every network in range. No fake SSID or credential capture is involved.
mcqs.context: An attacker floods a wireless frequency with noise so laptops in a warehouse cannot associate with any access point. The interference affects every network in range and is not tied to one SSID. The wireless team is naming the attack.

mcqs.prompt: Which capability should they adopt?

options.rationale: Correct choice — XDR: XDR extends detection across multiple layers.
Signature-based endpoint protection does not correlate telemetry across endpoint, network, and cloud.
A standalone firewall filters packets at one boundary and does not correlate telemetry across endpoint, network, and cloud.
A password manager stores credentials; it does not correlate endpoint, network, and cloud telemetry.

mcqs.explanation: XDR extends detection across multiple layers; AV is endpoint-only and does not correlate broadly. Why the other options fail: Traditional antivirus — Signature-based endpoint protection does not correlate telemetry across endpoint, network, and cloud.; A standalone firewall — A standalone firewall filters packets at one boundary and does not correlate telemetry across endpoint, network, and cloud.; A password manager — A password manager stores credentials; it does not correlate endpoint, network, and cloud telemetry.
mcqs.hint: The platform must combine endpoint, network, identity, and cloud telemetry. One layer alone is not enough.
mcqs.context: A security team wants one platform that correlates endpoint process data, network flows, identity events, and cloud audit logs into a single investigation. It is comparing products that each cover only one of those layers.

mcqs.prompt: A scanner reports dozens of findings. To prioritize, the team should FIRST consider which factor?

options.text: CVSS severity combined with asset criticality and exploitability
options.rationale: Correct choice — CVSS severity combined with asset criticality and exploitability: Risk-based prioritization weighs severity, asset value, and exploitability, not arbitrary ordering.
Alphabetical order has no relationship to risk.

options.text: The oldest finding by discovery date
options.rationale: Age alone does not reflect exposure, severity, or asset criticality.

options.text: The number of lines in the report
options.rationale: Report length is unrelated to the severity or exploitability of a finding.

mcqs.explanation: Risk-based prioritization weighs severity, asset value, and exploitability, not arbitrary ordering. Why the other options fail: The alphabetical order of hostnames — Alphabetical order has no relationship to risk.; The oldest finding by discovery date — Age alone does not reflect exposure, severity, or asset criticality.; The number of lines in the report — Report length is unrelated to the severity or exploitability of a finding.
mcqs.hint: Severity alone is not enough; an internet-facing payment system and an isolated lab host carry different exposure.
mcqs.context: A vulnerability scanner returns dozens of findings across production, staging, and development. The team has limited remediation time and needs a defensible order. It is choosing the first factor to weigh when ranking the findings.

mcqs.prompt: Which supply-chain attack is this?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Dependency confusion / typosquatting: Look-alike package names are typosquatting.
SQL injection manipulates a database query; it does not forge a domain-wide authentication ticket.
A distributed denial-of-service flood exhausts availability; it does not test credentials or capture a session.
Phishing is a broad message-based lure; it does not describe a forged pointer to a memory address.

mcqs.explanation: Look-alike package names are typosquatting; dependency confusion abuses internal/external resolution order. Why the other options fail: SQL injection — SQL injection manipulates a database query; it does not forge a domain-wide authentication ticket.; DDoS — A distributed denial-of-service flood exhausts availability; it does not test credentials or capture a session.; Phishing — Phishing is a broad message-based lure; it does not describe a forged pointer to a memory address.
mcqs.hint: The package name imitates a trusted internal library and runs an install script. That is an upstream dependency trick.
mcqs.context: A build pipeline installs a package whose name is almost identical to a popular internal library. The package was published by an unknown account and contains a post-install script that contacts an external host. The supply-chain team is naming the attack.

mcqs.prompt: Which protocol should be chosen?

options.rationale: Correct choice — WPA3 (SAE): WPA3 uses SAE (Dragonfly) to resist offline cracking.
WEP is broken and can be cracked quickly; it does not resist offline guessing.
The older TKIP-based standard has known weaknesses and does not use the modern handshake.
An open wireless network provides no encryption or authentication.

mcqs.explanation: WPA3 uses SAE (Dragonfly) to resist offline cracking; WEP and WPA are broken/weak. Why the other options fail: WEP — WEP is broken and can be cracked quickly; it does not resist offline guessing.; WPA (TKIP) — The older TKIP-based standard has known weaknesses and does not use the modern handshake.; Open — An open wireless network provides no encryption or authentication.
mcqs.hint: Compare handshakes, not version numbers. The newer one resists offline guessing even with a weak passphrase.
mcqs.context: A new wireless network must resist offline guessing against the handshake even if a user chooses a weak passphrase. The network team is comparing standards by their handshake design, not by marketing version numbers.

mcqs.prompt: A public web server, an internal database, and partner VPNs must be separated. Which design BEST limits lateral movement after a breach?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Microsegmentation with per-zone policy: Microsegmentation contains compromise.
A single flat network gives every host a path to every other host, which increases lateral movement.
Disabling the firewall removes a control instead of segmenting the network.
A DMZ exposes services to the internet; placing every host there increases exposure rather than limiting lateral movement.

mcqs.explanation: Microsegmentation contains compromise; a flat network lets an attacker roam freely. Why the other options fail: A single flat network — A single flat network gives every host a path to every other host, which increases lateral movement.; Disabling the firewall — Disabling the firewall removes a control instead of segmenting the network.; Putting everything in the DMZ — A DMZ exposes services to the internet; placing every host there increases exposure rather than limiting lateral movement.
mcqs.hint: The design must separate each workload and allow only the flows it needs, not just put a firewall at the edge.
mcqs.context: A public web server, an internal database, and a partner VPN concentrator share one flat network. A breach of the web server would let an attacker reach the database directly. The architect is choosing the segmentation design that limits lateral movement.

mcqs.prompt: A cloud app needs to let users log in with their corporate Google identity. Which solution provides this without sharing passwords?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Federation with SAML/OIDC: Federation lets an identity provider assert identity via tokens.
Storing passwords in the application increases credential exposure and does not federate identity.
Disabling single sign-on pushes passwords back into the application and increases credential exposure.
A shared account removes individual accountability and does not federate identity.

mcqs.explanation: Federation lets an identity provider assert identity via tokens; password sharing breaks SSO's whole point. Why the other options fail: Storing passwords in the app — Storing passwords in the application increases credential exposure and does not federate identity.; Disabling SSO — Disabling single sign-on pushes passwords back into the application and increases credential exposure.; Using a shared service account — A shared account removes individual accountability and does not federate identity.
mcqs.hint: The app must trust an external identity provider's assertion and never see the user's password.
mcqs.context: A cloud application must let users sign in with their existing corporate Google identity. The application must not receive or store the user's Google password. The developer is choosing the integration that provides this.

mcqs.prompt: Which authentication method is MOST resistant to phishing because it uses public-key cryptography and is not replayable?

options.rationale: Correct choice — FIDO2 / WebAuthn: FIDO2/WebAuthn is phishing-resistant via origin-bound keys.
SMS codes are replayable and phishable; they do not bind authentication to the site's origin.
A static password can be captured or reused and does not bind authentication to a website origin.
Security questions are knowledge-based secrets that can be researched or guessed and are not origin-bound.

mcqs.explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn is phishing-resistant via origin-bound keys; SMS OTP is vulnerable to interception. Why the other options fail: SMS one-time codes — SMS codes are replayable and phishable; they do not bind authentication to the site's origin.; A static password — A static password can be captured or reused and does not bind authentication to a website origin.; Security questions — Security questions are knowledge-based secrets that can be researched or guessed and are not origin-bound.
mcqs.hint: The method must bind the credential to the site's origin and use a key pair, so a captured assertion cannot be replayed elsewhere.
mcqs.context: An authentication standard must resist phishing and replay. The method must bind the credential to the website's origin and use public-key cryptography so a captured assertion cannot be reused elsewhere.

mcqs.prompt: Sensitive data must remain physically in the EU and under EU law. Which requirement addresses this?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Data residency / sovereignty: Data residency/sovereignty dictates where data is stored and which laws apply.
Tokenization replaces sensitive values with vaulted surrogates; it does not prove a package's publisher or satisfy a data-location requirement.
Hashing is one-way and cannot replace a card number that must be recovered for refunds; it also does not prove website identity.
Compression reduces size and provides no confidentiality; it also does nothing to satisfy data-location requirements.

mcqs.explanation: Data residency/sovereignty dictates where data is stored and which laws apply. Why the other options fail: Tokenization — Tokenization replaces sensitive values with vaulted surrogates; it does not prove a package's publisher or satisfy a data-location requirement.; Hashing — Hashing is one-way and cannot replace a card number that must be recovered for refunds; it also does not prove website identity.; Compression — Compression reduces size and provides no confidentiality; it also does nothing to satisfy data-location requirements.
mcqs.hint: Two ideas are combined: the data stays inside a border, and that nation's law governs it.
mcqs.context: A company sells to customers in the European Union and must keep their records physically inside the EU under EU law. The legal team is choosing the requirement that captures both the location and the governing jurisdiction.

mcqs.prompt: A cloud account keeps drifting into insecure settings. Which control would BEST provide continuous guardrails?

options.rationale: Correct choice — CSPM: CSPM continuously detects cloud misconfiguration.
A one-time test samples the environment at a moment in time and does not provide continuous cloud posture monitoring.
Disabling logging removes the evidence needed to detect drift and investigate incidents.
A spreadsheet depends on manual updates and does not continuously check cloud configuration.

mcqs.explanation: CSPM continuously detects cloud misconfiguration; a one-time test does not. Why the other options fail: A one-time penetration test — A one-time test samples the environment at a moment in time and does not provide continuous cloud posture monitoring.; Disabling logging — Disabling logging removes the evidence needed to detect drift and investigate incidents.; Manual spreadsheet tracking — A spreadsheet depends on manual updates and does not continuously check cloud configuration.
mcqs.hint: The control must continuously compare cloud configuration against a baseline and flag drift, not run once.
mcqs.context: A cloud account repeatedly drifts into insecure settings: a storage bucket becomes public, a security group opens a management port, and logging is disabled. The team wants continuous detection and guardrails, not a one-time audit.

mcqs.prompt: An analyst confirms a ransomware infection is actively encrypting files. What should they do FIRST?

options.text: Contain the affected segment to stop spread
options.rationale: Correct choice — Contain the affected segment to stop spread: Containment limits impact and is the immediate next step once an incident is confirmed.
Writing the report before containing the incident lets the damage continue.
A meeting reviews the incident; it does not stop files from being encrypted right now.
New hardware does not contain the active ransomware infection or stop its spread.

mcqs.explanation: Containment limits impact and is the immediate next step once an incident is confirmed. Why the other options fail: Write the final report — Writing the report before containing the incident lets the damage continue.; Schedule a lessons-learned meeting — A meeting reviews the incident; it does not stop files from being encrypted right now.; Order new laptops — New hardware does not contain the active ransomware infection or stop its spread.
mcqs.hint: Encryption is spreading to mapped drives. Stop the spread first; reporting and recovery come later.
mcqs.context: An analyst confirms that ransomware is actively encrypting files on a file server and spreading to mapped drives. The incident commander must choose the immediate next action before the encryption reaches backups.

mcqs.prompt: Disk images and RAM captures must be admissible in court. Which process is MOST critical to preserve?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Chain of custody: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when.
Encryption at rest protects stored data; it does not document who handled evidence.
Compression reduces size and provides no confidentiality; it also does nothing to satisfy data-location requirements.
A hash alone proves integrity but not who handled the evidence or when.

mcqs.explanation: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when; without it, admissibility is challenged. Why the other options fail: Encryption at rest — Encryption at rest protects stored data; it does not document who handled evidence.; Compression — Compression reduces size and provides no confidentiality; it also does nothing to satisfy data-location requirements.; Hashing only — A hash alone proves integrity but not who handled the evidence or when.
mcqs.hint: The court cares who handled the evidence and when. The record must be unbroken from seizure onward.
mcqs.context: Disk images and memory captures from a compromised host must be admissible in court. The forensic team is choosing the process that must be documented from seizure through analysis.

mcqs.prompt: A SIEM shows a single login from two countries within three minutes. Which control would BEST have flagged this automatically?

options.rationale: Correct choice — UEBA: UEBA baselines behavior and flags impossible-travel anomalies.
Antivirus signatures match known malicious files; they do not baseline account behavior across locations.
A firewall rule filters network traffic; it does not establish whether a behavior is normal for an account.
Password history prevents reuse; it does not detect an impossible-travel login.

mcqs.explanation: UEBA baselines behavior and flags impossible-travel anomalies; AV signatures target malware. Why the other options fail: Antivirus signatures — Antivirus signatures match known malicious files; they do not baseline account behavior across locations.; A firewall rule — A firewall rule filters network traffic; it does not establish whether a behavior is normal for an account.; Password history — Password history prevents reuse; it does not detect an impossible-travel login.
mcqs.hint: The pattern is a behavior anomaly across locations, not a known malware signature or a firewall rule.
mcqs.context: A SIEM shows one account logged in from two countries within three minutes. The account has no travel history and the locations are far apart. The SOC is choosing the control that should have flagged the pattern automatically.

mcqs.prompt: The team wants repetitive alerts like 'isolate host' to run without an analyst. Which capability should they deploy?

options.rationale: Correct choice — SOAR playbooks: SOAR automates response workflows.
A wiki documents steps for a human; it does not execute the response actions automatically.
A new firewall filters traffic; it does not execute a multi-step response workflow.
More alerts increase noise; they do not execute a response action.

mcqs.explanation: SOAR automates response workflows; manual wikis do not execute actions. Why the other options fail: Manual runbooks in a wiki — A wiki documents steps for a human; it does not execute the response actions automatically.; A new firewall — A new firewall filters traffic; it does not execute a multi-step response workflow.; More pager alerts — More alerts increase noise; they do not execute a response action.
mcqs.hint: The capability must execute a sequence of response actions from a trigger, not just display a runbook.
mcqs.context: The team wants repetitive, reversible alerts such as 'isolate this host' to run without waiting for an analyst. It is choosing the capability that can execute a sequence of response actions from a trigger.

mcqs.prompt: A system can tolerate at most 1 hour of downtime and 15 minutes of data loss. Which statement correctly applies these metrics to the backup design?

options.text: The backup frequency must satisfy the RPO of 15 minutes
options.rationale: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, so backups or replication must run at least every 15 minutes to bound the loss.

options.text: The backup frequency must satisfy the RTO of 15 minutes
options.rationale: RTO concerns how fast service is restored, not how much data may be lost. It does not set backup frequency.

options.text: The MTBF of 1 hour sets how often backups run
options.rationale: MTBF is the expected time between failures, a reliability statistic. It does not schedule backups.

options.text: The MTTR of 15 minutes is the maximum data loss allowed
options.rationale: MTTR is the average time to repair a failed component, not an amount of data.

mcqs.explanation: A maximum loss of 15 minutes of data is the recovery point objective, so replication or backups must run at least every 15 minutes. The one-hour downtime tolerance is the recovery time objective and governs how fast the service must come back, not how often backups run.
mcqs.hint: Match each stated limit to the metric it defines: outage time to one target, data loss to the other.
mcqs.context: A system can tolerate at most one hour of downtime and at most fifteen minutes of lost transactions. The team is choosing a backup and replication schedule that meets both limits without overbuilding the solution.

mcqs.prompt: Backups must survive a ransomware wipe of the primary array. Which design is MOST resilient?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Immutable, offline/air-gapped copies: Immutable and air-gapped backups cannot be altered by ransomware.
A snapshot on the compromised array can be encrypted or deleted along with the primary data.

options.text: Daily copies on the same array
options.rationale: Copies on the same array share the attacker's blast radius and can be wiped with the primary data.
Printed reports are stale snapshots and cannot be restored as a recovery copy.

mcqs.explanation: Immutable and air-gapped backups cannot be altered by ransomware; same-array copies can be encrypted too. Why the other options fail: A single on-array snapshot — A snapshot on the compromised array can be encrypted or deleted along with the primary data.; Daily copies on the same array — Copies on the same array share the attacker's blast radius and can be wiped with the primary data.; Printed reports — Printed reports are stale snapshots and cannot be restored as a recovery copy.
mcqs.hint: The attacker has the backup server's domain account. At least one copy must be outside that account's reach and unchangeable.
mcqs.context: Backups must survive a ransomware attack that wipes the primary storage array and compromises the backup server's domain account. The architect is choosing the design that keeps at least one recovery copy out of the attacker's reach.

mcqs.prompt: Which treatment is BEST?

options.rationale: Correct choice — Risk transfer (insurance): Transfer moves financial impact to a third party, typically via insurance.
Avoidance eliminates the activity; the scenario keeps the service and moves the cost.
Acceptance tolerates the exposure; the scenario shifts the financial impact to an insurer.
Mitigation reduces the exposure with a control; the scenario shifts the financial consequence.

mcqs.explanation: Transfer moves financial impact to a third party, typically via insurance; avoidance eliminates the activity. Why the other options fail: Risk avoidance — Avoidance eliminates the activity; the scenario keeps the service and moves the cost.; Risk acceptance — Acceptance tolerates the exposure; the scenario shifts the financial impact to an insurer.; Risk mitigation — Mitigation reduces the exposure with a control; the scenario shifts the financial consequence.
mcqs.hint: The service stays, but the financial consequence moves to a third party. That is a treatment choice, not a control.
mcqs.context: A risk cannot be removed without shutting down a profitable service, and insurance can absorb the financial impact. The risk committee is choosing the treatment that shifts the cost to a third party.

mcqs.prompt: Which BIA output drives the recovery target?

options.text: The recovery time objective derived from the $50k/hr impact
options.rationale: Correct choice — The recovery time objective derived from the $50k/hr impact: BIA quantifies impact to set RTO/RPO.
Headcount does not determine how much downtime a critical function can survive.
The hardware model does not determine the recovery time objective.
Office location does not determine the recovery target for a critical function.

mcqs.explanation: BIA quantifies impact to set RTO/RPO; the financial impact per hour drives the tolerance. Why the other options fail: The number of employees — Headcount does not determine how much downtime a critical function can survive.; The server model — The hardware model does not determine the recovery time objective.; The office location — Office location does not determine the recovery target for a critical function.
mcqs.hint: The BIA states how much downtime the business can survive. That becomes the recovery target.
mcqs.context: A critical function loses $50,000 for every hour it is down and can be restored in four hours. The business impact analysis must express the maximum acceptable outage as a recovery target.

mcqs.prompt: Which framework is REQUIRED?

options.rationale: Correct choice — CMMC 2.0: CMMC 2.0 is the DoD supply-chain maturity requirement.
The payment-card standard governs cardholder data; it is not the defense supply-chain maturity model.
The U.S. health-information law governs medical records; it is not the defense supply-chain maturity model.
The EU privacy regulation governs personal data; it is not the U.S. defense supply-chain maturity model.

mcqs.explanation: CMMC 2.0 is the DoD supply-chain maturity requirement; the others govern payments, health, and EU data. Why the other options fail: PCI DSS — The payment-card standard governs cardholder data; it is not the defense supply-chain maturity model.; HIPAA — The U.S. health-information law governs medical records; it is not the defense supply-chain maturity model.; GDPR — The EU privacy regulation governs personal data; it is not the U.S. defense supply-chain maturity model.
mcqs.hint: The requirement is specific to Department of Defense suppliers and has defined maturity levels.
mcqs.context: A U.S. defense contractor must prove a defined level of supply-chain cybersecurity maturity before it can bid on a contract. An accredited assessor will evaluate its practices against a Department of Defense model.

mcqs.prompt: A vendor will process customer PII. Which agreement MOST clearly allocates data-protection responsibilities?

options.rationale: Correct choice — A DPA (Data Processing Agreement): A DPA contractually defines processor responsibilities for personal data.
